lesson.title: The Temperament You Were Born With
lesson.summary: Temperament is the biologically based pattern of emotional reactivity and self-regulation that shows up almost from birth and forms the raw material personality is built from.
lesson.body:
Even in a hospital nursery, newborns do not all act alike. Some babies settle quickly after a diaper change, some fuss at the slightest disturbance, some sleep on a predictable schedule while others seem to have no schedule at all. Psychologists call these early, biologically based differences in emotional reactivity and self-regulation temperament. Unlike personality traits that develop through years of experience, temperament is visible almost from birth, which is one of the main pieces of evidence that it has a strong genetic and constitutional basis rather than being purely learned.

Temperament is a natural case study for the nature versus nurture debate, and the honest answer is that it is both. Genes appear to set a range for how reactive and how easily soothed a child tends to be, but environment, how caregivers respond to a fussy baby, how much stimulation a household provides, whether a culture values quiet children or expressive ones, shapes how that underlying reactivity gets expressed and regulated over time. Temperament is a starting point, not a fixed destiny.

The most influential early research on temperament came from Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess, whose long running New York Longitudinal Study followed children from infancy and rated them on dimensions like activity level, adaptability to new situations, mood, and intensity of reactions. From these ratings they described three broad, informal patterns: easy children, who adapted smoothly and generally had positive moods, difficult children, who were more intense, irregular, and slower to adapt, and slow to warm up children, who were initially withdrawn or wary but gradually became comfortable. A substantial share of the children in their sample did not fit neatly into any single category, a useful reminder that these are rough descriptive patterns rather than rigid boxes.

A second influential line of research, led by Jerome Kagan, focused on behavioral inhibition, how strongly infants react to new or unfamiliar stimuli. Kagan found that highly reactive infants, who showed more distress and motor activity in response to novelty, were somewhat more likely than low reactive infants to grow into shy or wary children. The relationship was real but far from deterministic. Many highly reactive infants did not become shy, which fits with the broader point that temperament describes a tendency, not a fixed outcome.

Temperament matters for development partly because it does not exist in a vacuum. As the next chapter explores, a child's temperament interacts constantly with how caregivers respond to that child, which is one reason the same parenting approach can work beautifully with one child and struggle with another.
